Whereas Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative brain disorder in the United States with symptoms that vary person to person and may include tremors, difficulty with balance, swallowing, chewing, and speaking, slowness of movement and rigidity, cognitive impairment and dementia, mood disorders, and a variety of other non-motor symptoms. And whereas Parkinson's disease is estimated to affect approximately 1 million people in the U.S. alone, and the prevalence will rise to 1.2 million by 2030. And whereas Parkinson's disease is the 14th leading cause of death in the United States, according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention. And whereas research suggests the cause of Parkinson's disease is a combination of genetic and environmental factors, but the exact cause and progression of the disease is still unknown, and there is no objective test or biomarker for the disease. And whereas there is no standard treatment for this disease, treatment for each person is based on his or her symptoms and may include medication, surgery, and lifestyle modifications, such as more rest and exercise, but no treatment as yet will reverse the effects of the disease. And whereas, according to the Michael J. Fox Foundation, the total cost of Parkinson's disease to individuals, families, and the U.S. government totals nearly $52 billion a year, which includes $26.5 billion of non-medical costs like missed work, lost wages, early forced retirement, and family caregiver time, demonstrating the devastating effects the disease has on person's finances and ability to participate in the labor market. And whereas Parkinson's disease affects not only the patient, but the patient's loved ones and caregivers. And whereas volunteers, researchers, caregivers, and medical professionals are working to improve the quality of life for persons living with Parkinson's disease and their families. And whereas increased education and research are desperately needed to find more effective and lasting treatment and ultimately a cure for this debilitating disease. Now, therefore, be it proclaimed that I, Mayor Shelley Brindle, and recognition of the need to bring awareness to the plight of Parkinson's patients and their families to hereby designate the month of April of 2021 as Parkinson's Awareness Month in the town of Westfield. Be it further proclaimed that I hereby encourage my fellow residents to visit the Parkinson's Disease Foundation website at parkinson.org and the Michael J. text: Hello, everybody. My name is Peter Goldberg. By day, I manage an energy efficiency emerging technologies team at Con Edison and by night, I am a member of the Westfield Green Team. As David said, tonight, I'm here to report out on the recent installation of low-east storm windows in Town Hall. As I'm sure many people on the council are aware, the administrative conference room is notorious for being too cold in the winter and too hot in the summer and the culprits are the large single-pane windows in that room. They let the heat in during the summer and they let the heat out during the winter and that not only makes the room uncomfortable for you guys, it also makes the furnace work harder and the AC work harder and that wastes energy and costs the town money. So, that's why the Green Team applied for a sustainable Jersey gardener grant to install low-east storm windows in Town Hall and the idea behind low-east storm windows is simple. If you have an inefficient drafty single-pane window and you stick an extra pane of glass on the inside, then you basically have a much more efficient double-pane window and the low-e or low emissivity coating is transparent. You can see through it just fine but it blocks UV rays and radiant heat which basically keeps the heat from getting through the window. So, the town used $6,075 of gardener grant money to buy seven quanta panel architectural low-east storm windows and install them in the administrative conference room and the mayor's conference room. Low-east storm windows cost much less than full window replacements and they're much less disruptive to building operations and the aesthetics of a historic building like Town Hall. The storm windows that were installed will save over 80 therms and 100 kilowatt hours per year for the next 30 years. More broadly, installing low-east storm windows helps make Westfield the leader in energy efficiency. By growing awareness of this important technology, Westfield's contributing to a measure that both saves energy and makes future electrification efforts much easier. So, I'd like to thank everybody for your time here and if you like those storm windows, I'd encourage you to consider installing them elsewhere on the town's properties.

The first I'd like to move for the adoption of general ordinance number 2211 on second reading and ordinance rescinding certain provisions of the town code for the town of Westfield. This is the one about the library. I just have some context on it, the library ordinance that we're considering tonight. And again, I think I said this before, but by way of background, years ago, Westfield implemented an ordinance that made it possible or made it a possible municipal offense to have an overdue library book. And as far as we can tell, that ordinance was thankfully never used to actually charge anyone with an offense. But the context underlying this decision to rescind the ordinance is that in 2019, the American Library Association passed a resolution calling on libraries nationwide to find a way to eliminate overdue fines because they found that those fines were a form of social inequity. And the association found that library users with limited income tend to stay away from libraries because they may be afraid of incurring debt. And then it stood to reason that these same users will also stay away if they have already incurred a fine simply because they don't have the money to pay it. And libraries in major cities all across the country have analyzed the effects of late fees and found that they disproportionately deter low income residents and children from actually coming to the library. And the effect of that is driving away the people who actually stand to benefit the most from free library resources. And of course, baked into that analysis was the fact that for many families, the library was the best source of computer and online internet access and resources, and it wasn't just simply about checking on books. And so based on the ALA's resolution, the library, the Westfield Library Board, weighed the facts and alternatives and made the decision to follow the ALA's guidance by choosing to eliminate the fees. And that's the decision that the board had the responsibility for. And in light of that, we thought it was best to eliminate an anachronism that I think we can all agree was unfairly punitive and was never enforced by the town in any event. So can we have a second, please? Second. Any discussion?

speaker: markp
text: I'd also like to move general ordinance number 2212 on second reading, an ordinance requiring the licensing and registration of landscapers within the town of Westfield and making certain amendments to the conservation center regulations. And Mayor, if it's okay, I'd like to kind of give some context with respect to this ordinance as well. Absolutely. So just to give everyone a quick update on the registration ordinance in order to provide a little bit of clarity on what's up for adoption this evening by the council. And I think it's necessary in part, given that I've seen some articles in the press recently that have conflated the intended purpose and effect of the registration ordinance with the concept of restricting, regulating, or banning the use of lawn and landscaping equipment and specifically the use of gas powered leaf blowers. So the landscape ordinance that we're addressing tonight came out of the co-review in town property committee after several discussions. And the purposes of the licensing and registration process is simple to provide the town with contact information about the landscapers and landscapers, by the way, includes tree removal businesses as well that are doing business in Westfield and to provide a method, the landscapers to provide a method to provide a landscapers or relevant town rules and regulations so that they understand the do's and don'ts of operating in the town. Among other things, registration allows the town to more effectively enforce the town's rules when it comes not just to storm debris, but also regarding invasive plants that are prohibited like bamboo, for example, and other rules like those related to setbacks. It also allows the town to more timely and effectively address specific resident concerns about a particular landscaping business and respond to complaints that are issued by residents. And registration also allows the town to efficiently and effectively update those landscapers as rules and regulations may change from time to time. Now, the fee for licensing itself is nominal for any commercial landscaper. It's $50 is about the same cost as three cans of gas. And it's been argued that the amount of the registration fee is not going to chase any landscaper away from doing business in Westfield under those circumstances. But that said, to mitigate the potential of any impact of the fee, we included a couple of key provisions in the new ordinance. First, the registration fees waived for any landscaper that's currently registered to use the conservation center to deposit their daily debris. And this is a great program that was started only a few years ago with just a handful of landscapers. And to date, I understand that more than 50 landscapers have registered this year. So for those landscapers, 50 different landscapers, there's no added cost for them to operate in the town because the fee is waived. Second, as Tom Jordan was saying earlier, we exempted non-commercial residents from the registration requirement. This is what I call basically the kid with a lawnmower exemption. The reason we included that was we don't want to discourage enterprising neighborhood kids from earning some summer money by mowing lawns. As for leaf blowers themselves, that's not part of the ordinance tonight, but we recognize that this is a quality of life issue. And it's something that the code review committee, public works committee in the town have been continually monitoring. I can say I've been on code review now for a year and a couple of months, and it's something that we address frequently. Just last June, we enacted an ordinance restricting the hours that those devices can be used. And that's an ordinance that it's something we can and continually do revisit. And moreover, we're also considering whether or not to implement additional restrictive measures. In fact, tonight's summits town council is considering a measure that would prohibit the use of blowers during certain summer months. Councilman Legripo, who's also on the code review committee, has forwarded to me some recent community comments and articles towards that end regarding a handful of other towns that have considered and or implemented those kinds of measures. But before we take any steps in that direction, we want to make sure that an appropriate balance, we strike an appropriate balance and they're all stakeholders. And that's not just landscapers, but it's also the myriad of homeowners who maintain their own lawns have a chance to weigh in on the issue. As far as the the landscaper who lives in Cranford or somewhere else and operates a business, he has to register. It's a $50 fee. But there's no it's just a registration process. And that's it. To sum it up, if and when we do implement any additional measures or restrictions, as far as the use of gas blowers or anything else. Tonight's registration ordinance is going to allow us to promptly inform the vast majority of those landscapers who operate in this town, and then to reasonably enforce those changes as soon as possible.
